latest.summary: Tracked expert Lance Fortnow says rumors about cryptography are circulating and advises monitoring the RSA Challenge factoring problems as early indicators, with fast progress such as factoring 1536-bit numbers being the alarm threshold.

A commenter relays unverified social-media rumours that OpenAI and Anthropic have found factoring in P, that P=BQP has been proven, that ECC is broken and that Ring-LWE is not quantum-resistant, with no evidence or personal endorsement given.

A retweet of an unverified rumour that frontier AI labs have broken major cryptographic primitives, including 'factoring is in P', with no evidence in the visible text and no sign the retweeter endorses it or is alarmed.

A retweet of @zkDragon's commentary on circulating cryptography-break rumours, which appears to downplay them (factoring only connects to pairings, and even a 1-billion-factor speedup 'still…' falls short), but the text is truncated and no actual break claim is verified.

The author says a hypothetical proof that factoring is in P would not change their beliefs, since factoring has so much structure that it seems surprising it is not already in P, and it would not affect their belief that learning parity with noise is hard; this is a hypothetical, with no break claimed or reported.

A commenter hypothesizes how someone with an efficient elliptic curve discrete log algorithm could profit secretly (e.g., minting Monero, stealing old coins) and suggests signals to monitor, without claiming any real break.

A commenter speculates that an AI-found classical elliptic-curve discrete log break (ECDSA, with Bitcoin as a casualty) is plausible and hopes for responsible disclosure, but cites no evidence and claims no actual break.
An ordinary commenter predicts, without evidence, that frontier AI labs will be confirmed to have methods that break SHA256 and other common cryptography.
A routine eprint proves tight post-quantum security bounds for Ascon AEAD under nonce misuse, with matching quantum attacks at O(2^{c/3}) queries that do not break the standard security claims.

An ePrint paper proves stronger security bounds (near-n-bit rather than birthday-scale) for preimage and second-preimage resistance of the JH hash mode in the ideal-permutation model, which is a strengthening result and not a break.

An eprint analyzes the 'target quotient' technique against homogeneous MQ signature schemes (UOV, SNOVA, QR-UOV), reporting only marginal attack-cost savings of about 0.05-4.6 bits, so no practical break and no urgent action is implied.

An eprint paper presents MechCrypto, an LLM-agent cryptanalysis tool that reports 23 Critical findings across 119 first-round NGCC candidates, including a zero-search collision in the MEGASCON AVX-512 S-box. These are flaws in new competition submissions, not breaks of deployed standards such as RSA, ECC, or established hashes.
Nic Carter relays a crowdsourced guess that an unspecified rumoured development is a theoretical quantum attack on lattice-based post-quantum cryptography.
Tracked expert @nic_carter relays, secondhand and unverified, that 'chat' thinks a linked item is a quantum attack on Ring-LWE, a lattice assumption.

An eprint shows the Distorted McEliece Public Key assumption of Dyseryn-Francati-Venturi pseudorandom codes is false for full-support Raw Reed-Solomon codes, since a parity check distinguishes the key, but it gives no key recovery or ciphertext-level break and does not affect standard deployed cryptography.

An ePrint paper proves worst-case (2,1)-quasi-cyclic syndrome decoding is NP-complete for low weight (w < sqrt(n)) via reduction from 3-Dimensional Matching. This is a theoretical hardness result that supports code-based cryptography (e.g., BIKE/HQC) and does not claim any break.

An eprint paper presents an incremental optimization of critical-pair selection in the F4 Gröbner basis algorithm, cutting MQ-solving time by 35-67% on small weakly overdetermined instances over F_31; this is routine algorithmic work with no claimed break of any cryptosystem.
A commenter gives a general explanation that factoring is in NP and coNP, so it is not believed NP-complete and could be in P even if P≠NP; it reports no break.

The author argues that P vs NP debates are meaningless for practical security, noting that even a hypothetical polynomial-time factoring algorithm with a huge exponent like O((log n)^25) wouldn't weaken RSA in practice, and does not claim any actual break.

The author argues that P vs NP debates are irrelevant to practical security, noting that even a hypothetical polynomial-time factoring algorithm with a huge exponent like O((log n)^25) would leave RSA's real-world security unchanged, and does not claim or report any actual break.

A commenter (not Aaronson) on a post about a VP ≠ VNP result argues that P ≠ NP is not close, says an effective P = NP would be a sudden but unlikely bombshell, and reports no break of any cryptographic primitive.

A commenter named Jeff argues in general terms that P≠NP (or P=NP) would not by itself settle practical cryptographic security, given constants, non-constructive proofs and similar caveats, and makes no claim of an actual break.
A commenter asks Scott Aaronson whether circulating, less-confident break rumours concern only RSA or also touch post-quantum protocols, without reporting a specific break themselves.
A commenter sarcastically speculates that frontier AI labs have secretly broken unspecified cryptographic protocols and profit from forcing everyone onto replacements.

The tracked expert relays Scott Aaronson's statements that a major cryptographic breakthrough is expected to be disclosed soon, that it does not immediately threaten RSA, and that rumours of more consequential breaks persist.

A commenter links an eprint (2026/3020) claiming a deterministic subexponential-time discrete log algorithm and remarks on it casually, without urging action; the rest of the comment is unrelated complexity-theory talk.
